summary: Describes an architecture for securing Internet routing, built on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure. The RPKI reflects how IP address space and AS numbers are allocated, and a distributed repository stores the signed objects. A first use is letting the holder of address space authorize which network may originate routes for it. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Who owns an internet address? This explains a system of digital certificates that proves it, so a network can show it is allowed to announce an address, like a deed at a registry.

questions: how to secure bgp route origin
what is a route origination authorization
how does rpki secure bgp origin
subtitle: How signed certificates tied to IP address allocations let a network prove it may announce a route.

tldr.problem: BGP assumes the network that originates a route for an address prefix is allowed to do so, but nothing in the Internet lets anyone verify that claim.
tldr.mechanism: A public key infrastructure mirrors the hierarchy of IP address and AS number allocation. Address holders use it to sign Route Origination Authorizations, and a distributed repository holds those signed objects for anyone to download and check.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can validate who is authorized to originate a prefix and use that to build BGP route filters more securely. The RFC is informational and describes the architecture; companion documents hold the detailed profiles.

today: RFC 6480 was published in February 2012 as an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the architecture; the detailed profiles live in companion RFCs such as RFC 6482 and RFC 6486.

sections.title: The Architecture and Its Three Parts
sections.content:
RFC 6480 describes an architecture to support improved security for BGP routing. It has three principal elements: the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), digitally signed routing objects, and a distributed repository system that holds both the PKI objects and the signed routing objects.

The architecture lets an entity verifiably assert that it is the legitimate holder of a set of IP addresses or Autonomous System (AS) numbers. As its initial application, a holder of address space can explicitly and verifiably authorize one or more ASes to originate routes to that space. Such authorizations could be used, for example, to more securely construct BGP route filters.

The design reuses existing standards: the X.509 certificate profile from RFC 5280, the IP address and AS number extensions from RFC 3779, and Cryptographic Message Syntax from RFC 5652. It applies to IPv4 and IPv6 only; other uses, such as MPLS labels, are out of scope.
sections.eli5: There are three pieces: a set of ownership certificates, signed permission slips, and a public shelf where everything is stored so anyone can look.

sections.title: A PKI That Mirrors Address Allocation
sections.content:
IP address allocation is already hierarchical. The root is IANA, below it are five Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), and below those may sit National Internet Registries (NIRs), Local Internet Registries (LIRs) or ISPs, and subscribers. A certificate in the RPKI attests to one allocation, and issuing a subordinate certificate corresponds to sub-allocating addresses.

These resource certificates bind a public key to the addresses or AS numbers listed in the RFC 3779 extensions. They do not say who the subject is. The RFC states that the PKI provides authorization, not authentication, so subject names are not meant to be descriptive. A CA certificate's subject name is chosen by the issuer, must include the CommonName attribute, and must be unique among the subjects of that CA. The RFC suggests using something like an internal database key, which also limits the issuer's legal liability.

Each relying party (RP) picks its own trust anchors. IANA and the five RIRs are the obvious defaults, but an RP may create its own, for example to cover private address space (RFC 1918). An RP that does so may miss allocation errors, but the weakness stays local to that RP.
sections.eli5: The certificates follow the same family tree as who gave addresses to whom. They say what you hold, not who you are, like a ticket that says seat 12 without a name on it.

sections.title: End-Entity Certificates and Route Origination Authorizations
sections.content:
A CA certificate is needed by any holder who sub-allocates, and also by any holder who wants to issue ROAs, because the CA must issue the end-entity (EE) certificate that validates each ROA. An EE certificate's key does not sign other certificates. For ROAs and manifests, each EE certificate signs exactly one object, so the key can be destroyed after use and the object can be revoked simply by revoking its EE certificate.

A Route Origination Authorization (ROA) states that the holder of a set of prefixes has authorized one AS to originate routes for them. Its content is an AS number, a list of IP address prefixes and, optionally for each prefix, the maximum length of more specific prefixes the AS may also advertise. The ROA format is in RFC 6482 and the signed-object template is in RFC 6488.

A ROA holds a single AS number, so a holder who wants several ASes authorized must issue several ROAs. A ROA also cannot combine allocations from different sources, since it is tied to one EE certificate. The ROA is valid only while that EE certificate is valid, and its prefixes must exactly match those in the certificate's RFC 3779 extension.

There is no independent way to revoke a ROA. Revoking the EE certificate is the only mechanism.
sections.eli5: A ROA is a signed note saying this network may announce this address. Each note gets its own one-time pen, so tearing up the pen's certificate cancels the note.

sections.title: Repositories, Manifests and Local Caches
sections.content:
The repository system is described as the untrusted clearing-house for signed objects that must be globally accessible. It is one system made of many databases spread across registries. For every certificate there is a directory that is the authoritative publication point for the objects verifiable with it. The certificate's Subject Information Access (SIA) extension points to that directory, and a certificate's Authority Information Access (AIA) extension points to its issuer's certificate. Relying parties pull data at whatever pace they choose; the repository has no push mechanism. All publication points MUST be accessible via rsync, and operators may support other protocols as well.

Because the repository is untrusted, signatures reveal tampering, and manifests reveal deletion or replacement with stale data. A manifest lists the file name and a hash for each unexpired certificate, CRL or ROA from an authority. It carries a manifest number, the issue time, the time of the next planned update and the list of name and hash pairs (see RFC 6486).

To build a local cache, a relying party downloads the objects, verifies each manifest's signature and that it has not passed its nextUpdate time, checks that the files match the manifest hashes and none are missing, and then validates each EE certificate to its configured trust anchors. If hashes mismatch or files are missing, it notifies the repository administrator. After the first sync it can fetch only what changed.
sections.eli5: The public shelf is not guarded, so each shelf has a checklist of exactly which signed papers should be there. If a paper is missing or swapped for an old one, you notice by comparing against the list.

sections.title: Everyday Operations: Issuing, Rolling Keys and Managing ROAs
sections.content:
Certificates come out of normal allocation. A holder of provider-independent address space needs a CA certificate so it can issue ROAs to its ISPs. A CA that changes its key MUST perform a key rollover, following the conservative procedure in RFC 6489. Rollover is not needed when a new certificate reuses the same key, for example when a resource is gained or the validity period is extended.

To authorize an AS, the holder creates an EE certificate containing the prefixes, builds the ROA payload with those prefixes and the AS number, signs it with the EE key, and uploads both to the repository. Revoking a ROA means revoking its EE certificate through a CRL. The RFC warns to follow make before break: before revoking a ROA for a prefix that should stay routable, make sure another valid ROA lists that prefix and that its AS is actually originating the routes.

Who issues ROAs depends on the subscriber. A single-homed subscriber with addresses from its ISP is not in the RPKI at all, since the ISP issues ROAs for its more general prefixes. A multi-homed subscriber with its own AS number has two RECOMMENDED options: the primary ISP gives it a CA certificate so it issues its own ROA, or the ISP issues a ROA on its behalf. Having the primary ISP issue ROAs for secondary ISPs is NOT RECOMMENDED because it yields inconsistent origin AS numbers. A holder of portable address space MUST authorize one or more ASes with EE certificates and ROAs.
sections.eli5: When you give someone permission to announce your address, you write a new signed note first and cancel the old one only after the new one works, so there is never a gap.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that security considerations run through the whole document. The protections depend on the integrity and availability of the infrastructure. Object integrity comes from repository access controls: it is RECOMMENDED that only the issuers of signed objects may add, delete or modify them. Relying parties can detect tampering, but the RFC prefers that the repository prevent it where possible.

The repository is a distributed database, so it should be inherently resistant to denial-of-service attacks. The RFC still recommends replication and backup of the databases and physical security for the servers. IANA's role in the RPKI is covered in RFC 6491.
sections.eli5: Only the person who wrote a paper may put it on or take it off the shelf, and the shelf is copied in many places so one break-in cannot ruin it.
